transcript.text: Alright, everyone. Let's get started. As we all know, we're facing a trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit from a former employee, and the complaint is seeking broad inspection of our devices and systems. The case-management conference is next month, and no discovery has been exchanged yet. Our priorities are clear: protect the company's confidential information and keep defense costs under control. Before I approve the initial defense plan, I need each of you to identify any facts that should shape our approach. Discovery counsel, let's start with you -- what do we need to know or flag before we build out our discovery strategy? And insurance-coverage counsel, please chime in with anything relevant on your end as well.
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: Elena, I need to flag something important from my forensic review of the former employee's company laptop. The review confirmed that exactly three identified trade-secret files were copied to the device. Critically, the review found no customer data on the device and no evidence of any additional copying beyond those three files. My report is currently awaiting final partner review and has not yet been added to the case plan. This should significantly shape our discovery strategy -- it narrows the scope of what we need to address and gives us leverage to push back against the broad inspection demands in the complaint.

transcript.text: Elena, I need to flag several critical insurance coverage facts that will directly impact our defense plan and cost control. I've reviewed the applicable policy endorsement, and here's what it says: First, the trade-secret defense is covered, but subject to a $75,000 self-insured retention -- so the company will bear the first $75,000 in defense costs before insurer coverage kicks in. Second, we are required to use insurer-approved panel counsel for coverage to apply. Third, and this is critical for discovery planning, we must obtain written insurer consent before engaging any forensic vendor. The endorsement itself is currently stored in the risk department's file and has not been attached to this matter yet. These requirements need to be factored into our defense plan immediately -- especially the panel counsel and forensic vendor consent requirements, which could affect Samir's forensic work and our vendor engagements.

transcript.text: Thank you both. This is exactly what I needed to hear before approving any plan. Samir, your forensic findings are very significant -- the fact that only three identified trade-secret files were copied, with no customer data and no additional copying, gives us strong grounds to push back against the broad inspection demands. That report needs to get through partner review and into the case plan immediately. Morgan, your insurance flags are equally critical. The $75,000 self-insured retention means we need to be cost-conscious from day one, especially since the company bears those first costs directly. The panel counsel requirement and the forensic vendor consent requirement are both things we need to address right now -- Samir, I need to know whether your forensic work was done by a vendor that has insurer approval, because if not, we may have a coverage issue we need to cure. Morgan, can you get that endorsement attached to this matter today? And I want both of you to coordinate on making sure any forensic vendor engagement going forward has written insurer consent before we proceed. Before I settle on the final defense plan, I need to confirm: Samir, is your forensic report based on work that's already been completed, or is there additional forensic work pending? And Morgan, are there any other coverage conditions in that endorsement we should be aware of beyond what you've already flagged?
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: Elena, to answer your question directly: the forensic review of the former employee's company laptop is already completed. The findings I described -- the three identified trade-secret files copied, no customer data, and no evidence of additional copying -- are all from work that's been done. What remains is the final partner review of my report, and then it needs to be formally added to the case plan. There is no additional forensic work pending at this time. On the vendor question you raised -- I want to be transparent that I need to confirm whether the forensic work was performed by an insurer-approved vendor or whether it was done internally. I don't have that information in front of me right now, and I agree with you that we need to resolve that immediately given Morgan's flag about the written insurer consent requirement. Morgan, can you confirm whether the endorsement's forensic vendor consent requirement applies retroactively to work already completed, or only to future engagements? That distinction will tell us whether we have a coverage issue to cure or simply a going-forward compliance step. Either way, I'll coordinate with Morgan to make sure any further forensic vendor engagement has written insurer consent before we proceed.

So the most prudent course of action is to notify the insurer about the completed forensic work as soon as possible, seek their written acknowledgment or consent, and make absolutely sure any future forensic vendor engagement obtains written insurer consent in advance. I'll get the endorsement attached to this matter today, and I'll also initiate contact with the insurer to address the forensic vendor issue and confirm our panel counsel status.
